source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: With an oracle label deciding when to stop, self-correction looks good. Without labels (intrinsic), accuracy falls on the benchmarks tested.
quote: without the use of oracle labels, self-correction consistently results in a decrease in performance
limits: Generic 'review your answer' prompts. Single-answer tasks. Table text was garbled by pdftotext; row pairing is my best reading.
agent_relevance: A premortem prompt with no outside check will likely behave like intrinsic self-correction and can hurt. Any premortem step needs a code-side check or a stop rule that is not the model's own judgment.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Why it falls: the model cannot judge its own reasoning, so it flips right answers to wrong ones more often than the reverse.
numbers: GPT-3.5 on GSM8K kept its first answer 74.7% of the time over two rounds; among changes, correct->incorrect was more common than incorrect->correct. GPT-4 and GPT-4-Turbo changed answers less often.
limits: Mechanism inferred from answer-change counts, not from probing the model.
agent_relevance: Log answer flips in any premortem arm. A premortem on a confident answer may only add risk of flipping it.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Multi-agent debate does not clearly beat self-consistency at equal numbers of responses.
numbers: Table 7, GSM8K, GPT-3.5: 1 response 76.7; later rows 82.5, 83.2, 85.3, 83.0, 88.2 for debate and self-consistency at 3, 6 and 9 responses. Text: debate only slightly better than self-consistency at 3 responses; self-consistency better at larger counts.
limits: Column pairing in the table is garbled; I rely on the text.
agent_relevance: Any premortem arm should be compared with the same compute spent on extra samples. That is the fair control.

source: Tyen et al. (2024) LLMs cannot find reasoning errors, but can correct them given the error location
finding: Models are bad at finding the first wrong step in a reasoning trace, even when the error is objective. They are good at fixing it once told where it is.
numbers: BIG-Bench Mistake, 5 tasks. GPT-4, best model, reached 52.87% overall with direct step prompting. Tracking shuffled objects: GPT-4 62.29 (trace) / 65.33 (step) / 90.67 (CoT step); GPT-3.5-Turbo 10.10 / 1.67 / 19.00. Logical deduction GPT-4 40.67 / 67.67 / 10.33.
quote: state-of-the-art LLMs currently cannot find mistakes reliably
limits: Traces come from PaLM 2 Unicorn with CoT; label split skewed to wrong traces. Prompt style trades accuracy on right versus wrong traces.
agent_relevance: Tests the 'impasse trigger' idea directly: finding the fault is the bottleneck, not repair. A premortem must yield faults that code can locate and test.

source: Tyen et al. (2024) LLMs cannot find reasoning errors, but can correct them given the error location
finding: Gold error location lifts accuracy a lot. A random location also helps wrong traces but costs right ones.
numbers: Absolute change in accuracy after backtracking, with gold location: +18 to +44 points on originally wrong traces; 0 to -11 on originally right traces (multistep arithmetic -6.67/+43.92; Dyck -11.43/+36.86). Random location: wrong traces +5 to +22, right traces -9 to -16. A small classifier trained on out-of-domain data found mistakes better than prompting a large model.
limits: Gold labels are an oracle. The classifier needed training data from other tasks.
agent_relevance: A premortem that names a specific failing step gives repair what it lacks. A vague 'it might fail' acts like the random-location case, which loses correct answers.

source: Kamoi et al. (2024) When Can LLMs Actually Correct Their Own Mistakes? A Critical Survey of Self-Correction of LLMs
finding: Critical survey of self-correction. Separates feedback generation from refinement. Finds no prior work with successful self-correction from prompted-LLM feedback in general tasks.
numbers: Three headline findings: (1) no prior work shows successful self-correction from prompted LLM feedback except in tasks exceptionally suited to it (e.g. decomposable responses); (2) it works well when reliable external feedback exists; (3) large-scale fine-tuning enables it.
quote: no prior work shows reliable evidence of successful self-correction with in-context learning
limits: A survey. Marks many papers as unrealistic for using oracle labels or weak initial prompts.
agent_relevance: Supports the external-check rule. A premortem is a feedback-generation step, so it falls under finding (1).

source: Gou et al. (2024) CRITIC: LLMs can self-correct with tool-interactive critiquing
finding: Verification with a tool (search, code interpreter) helps. The same loop without the tool is unstable and can hurt.
numbers: ChatGPT: +7.7 F1 over three QA tasks, +7.0% absolute over three math tasks, 79.2% lower toxicity probability. Without the interpreter on text-davinci-003: a 1.8 point drop on a math task.
quote: exclusive reliance on self-correction without external feedback may yield modest improvements or even deteriorate performance
limits: Gains depend on tool quality. Self-Refine on Codex was reported as worse than tool-based correction.
agent_relevance: Same lesson from another angle: test the failure list from a premortem with code or retrieval, not by asking the model again.

source: Madaan et al. (2023) Self-Refine: iterative refinement with self-feedback
finding: Positive result for self-feedback on open-ended tasks: about 20% absolute average gain over 7 tasks with GPT-3.5, ChatGPT and GPT-4.
numbers: GPT-4: sentiment reversal 3.8 -> 36.2; code readability 15.0 -> 45.0; code optimization 92.9 -> 93.1 (+0.2). GPT-3.5 math reasoning 64.1 -> 64.1 (0 gain).
limits: Largest gains on style or preference tasks judged by an LLM or humans; none on math. Huang et al. attribute part of the gain to weak baseline prompts.
agent_relevance: Self-critique helps where no single right answer exists. Weak fit for the verify and impasse job we want from a premortem.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion: language agents with verbal reinforcement learning
finding: After a failed trial, the agent writes a lesson in words and tries again. Large gains when the failure signal is real (test results, environment reward).
numbers: HumanEval pass@1 91% vs 80% for GPT-4. ALFWorld: ReAct+Reflexion completed 130 of 134 tasks, +22% absolute over 12 steps; HotPotQA +20%; ReAct-only agent stuck at a 22% hallucination rate. Ablation on the 50 hardest HumanEval Rust problems: base 0.60; self-reflection without test generation 0.52; test generation without reflection 0.60; both 0.68.
limits: Needs a failure signal. MBPP Python false-positive test pass rate 16.3% vs 1.4% on HumanEval, so Reflexion scored below baseline on MBPP.
agent_relevance: Reflexion is retrospective: failure already happened. A premortem imagines failure before any signal. The ablation shows reflection without a test signal fell to 0.52, below the 0.60 baseline.

source: Renze and Guven (2024) Self-Reflection in LLM Agents: Effects on Problem-Solving Performance
finding: Nine LLMs re-answered multiple-choice questions they got wrong, using eight kinds of self-generated reflection. All helped; richer reflection helped more.
numbers: GPT-4 accuracy on re-asked items: baseline 0.786; Retry 0.827; Keywords 0.832; Advice 0.840; Instructions 0.849; Explanation 0.876; Solution 0.925; Composite 0.932; Unredacted (answer leaked) 0.971. GPT-3.5 Turbo 0.596 -> 0.827 composite; Llama 2 7b 0.297 -> 0.427.
limits: Reflection ran only on items already marked wrong, so the model was told it failed. That is the premortem premise, but with ground truth. Bare 'Retry' gained 4.1 points for GPT-4.
agent_relevance: Part of the effect is just being told the first answer was wrong. A premortem asserts failure without evidence, so the gain may be smaller or negative. Test it as its own arm.

source: Dhuliawala et al. (2023) Chain-of-Verification reduces hallucination in LLMs
finding: Plan verification questions, answer them independently of the draft, then revise. Answering without the draft in view works best.
numbers: Llama 65B biographies, FACTSCORE: few-shot 55.9; CoVe joint 60.8; factored 63.7; factor+revise 71.4. Wikidata list precision 0.17 -> 0.36; hallucinated answers 2.95 -> 0.68. MultiSpanQA F1 0.39 -> 0.48.
limits: Factual recall tasks. Joint variant worse because the model repeats its own earlier errors.
agent_relevance: Close cousin of premortem: write doubts as questions, then check them in fresh context. Run each failure story in a clean call.

source: Weng et al. (2023) LLMs are better reasoners with self-verification
finding: Backward verification: hide a condition from the question, plug in the candidate answer, and see if the model recovers the hidden value. Choose the candidate that verifies.
numbers: Average gain of 2.33% on InstructGPT; arithmetic tasks gained 1.67%/2.84% on average, other reasoning tasks 0.62%/0.78%. New state of the art on six of eight datasets.
limits: Small gains. Works best where a condition can be masked, i.e. arithmetic.
agent_relevance: Backward check from a stated outcome is the nearest formal analogue of 'assume the end, work backward', but gains are small outside arithmetic.

source: Chen et al. (2025) Reverse Thinking Makes LLMs Stronger Reasoners (RevThink)
finding: Train a student on forward reasoning plus a backward question and backward reasoning. This is training, not a prompt.
numbers: 12 datasets: average +13.53% over student zero-shot and +6.84% over the best distillation baseline. 10% of forward data beat plain fine-tuning on 10x more on StrategyQA. Mistral +12.68%, Gemma +14.37%.
limits: Needs fine-tuning, which our agent does not do. Backward reasoning here means question inversion, not imagining failure.
agent_relevance: Shows the backward direction carries signal only when trained in. Not evidence for a prompt-only premortem.

source: Saunders et al. (2022) Self-critiquing models for assisting human evaluators
finding: Fine-tuned critique models help humans find flaws. Models may hold knowledge of flaws that they do not state as critiques.
numbers: Assisted labelers found about 50% more flaws than unassisted; with deliberately misleading answers, assisted labelers found the intended flaws 50% more often. Critiques found on 54% of inputs unassisted vs 78% assisted. Larger models were better at self-critiquing.
limits: Trained critics; summarization; human in the loop.
agent_relevance: Critique lags recognition. A premortem prompt asks for critique-style output, which may fall short of what the model can recognise. Pair it with a recognise-and-check step.

source: McAleese et al. (2024) LLM critics help catch LLM bugs (CriticGPT)
finding: RLHF-trained critic writes bug reports on code. Catches more inserted bugs than paid human reviewers, but hallucinates and nitpicks more.
numbers: Critiques preferred over human critiques in 63% of cases on naturally occurring LLM errors, and over 80% on the inserted-bug set. Human+CriticGPT teams wrote more comprehensive critiques than humans alone, with fewer hallucinations than the model alone. Force Sampling Beam Search trades comprehensiveness against spurious issues.
limits: Needs training; code domain; contractors, not experts. Hallucinated bugs can mislead humans.
agent_relevance: Model-written failure lists contain false alarms. Premortem output needs a filter, either a test or a ranking step. Breadth versus false positives is the main design knob.

source: Kambhampati et al. (2024) LLMs can't plan, but can help planning in LLM-Modulo frameworks
finding: Position paper with data: LLMs alone do not plan or self-verify well. LLM proposes, a bank of external sound critics checks, a back-prompt controller returns the critiques.
numbers: About 12% of GPT-4 plans were executable and goal-reaching in autonomous mode (planning domains). Tree-of-Thoughts gains tied to external verifiers; the LLM's own criticisms 'are often quite off the mark'.
quote: LLMs can't plan, but can help planning
limits: Formal planning domains with models; not open-ended human-style planning.
agent_relevance: Design pattern for premortem: model proposes failure modes, hard critics (code, simulators, tests) decide.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Which agent causes task failures and when? (Who&When)
finding: After a multi-agent run has failed, LLMs are poor at saying which agent and which step caused it. This is the hindsight direction, the easier one.
numbers: 127 failed multi-agent systems. Best method: 53.5% accuracy for the responsible agent, 14.2% for the decisive step. Some methods did worse than random. o1 and DeepSeek R1 also not practical.
limits: Long logs; annotators disagreed 15% to 30% of the time on some items.
agent_relevance: If naming the cause of a real failure is this hard, naming it before failure is harder. Score premortem output against later outcomes; do not trust it.

source: Cemri et al. (2025) Why do multi-agent LLM systems fail? (MAST)
finding: Taxonomy of 14 failure modes in 3 groups, built from 150 traces with annotator kappa 0.88. LLM annotator reaches kappa 0.77 and 94% accuracy.
numbers: Failure rates of 41% to 86.7% across 7 open-source multi-agent systems. Modes include disobeying task specification, step repetition, loss of conversation history, no or incomplete verification, premature termination, reasoning-action mismatch. A role-order fix in ChatDev gave +9.4% task success.
limits: Failure patterns from open-source frameworks; not a test of premortem.
agent_relevance: A ready failure checklist to seed a premortem. Several modes (repetition, history loss, termination without verification) can be checked by code.

source: Gu et al. (2025) Is your LLM secretly a world model of the internet? (WebDreamer)
finding: Agent imagines the outcome of each candidate action with an LLM world model, scores it, then acts. A forward-simulation relative of premortem.
numbers: VisualWebArena: 34.1% relative gain over reactive baseline, slightly below tree search at 4 to 5 times lower cost. Online-Mind2Web +42.3% relative; Mind2Web-Live +23.8% relative. Trained Dreamer-7B beat Qwen2-VL-7B by 4.7% (VWA), 4.0% (Online-Mind2Web), 4.8% (Mind2Web-Live).
limits: Simulates single actions, not 'assume the whole plan failed'. Gains are against reactive baselines.
agent_relevance: Imagined outcomes before acting can beat reactive acting on real web tasks, when a value function ranks them.

source: Perez et al. (2022) Red teaming language models with language models
finding: One LM writes test cases that make a target LM fail. Machine red teaming at scale. Generation method changes yield and diversity a lot.
numbers: 0.5M zero-shot test cases drew offensive replies 3.7% of the time (18,444 failures). RL red LM with KL weight 0.3 drew offensive replies over 40% of the time, but 78% of its cases contained the word 'invisible', so diversity collapsed. Supervised and few-shot variants kept more diversity at lower yield.
limits: Failure detector is an offensiveness classifier; domain is toxic output.
agent_relevance: Machine red teaming works when a detector exists. Optimising hit rate collapses diversity, so a premortem generator needs a separate prompt per failure class.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Language models (mostly) know what they know
finding: Larger models are well calibrated on multiple choice and true/false in the right format. They can estimate P(True) for their own answer and P(IK) that they know it.
numbers: P(True) improves when the model sees many of its own samples. P(IK) calibration is weaker on new tasks. No single headline figure recorded.
limits: Format dependent; replacing an option with 'None of the above' hurts calibration.
agent_relevance: Cheap trigger: use P(True) or sample disagreement to decide when to run a premortem, instead of running it always.

source: Wikipedia 'Pre-mortem' and Klein (2007) 'Performing a project premortem'
finding: Not opened this session. Context only: the SUBFIELDS row cites Klein 2007 via Wikipedia and notes the page gives no outcome evidence.
numbers: none
limits: Not read by me; do not rely on this line.
agent_relevance: Human-side evidence belongs to other angles of this subfield.

source: Search gap record
finding: No LLM paper that explicitly tests a premortem or prospective-hindsight prompt was found. WebSearch budget was spent and Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex and arXiv search returned 429.
numbers: none
limits: Absence is not proof. Closest tested methods found: self-critique, Reflexion, CoVe, WebDreamer, machine red teaming.
agent_relevance: Treat a premortem arm in our own bench as an open experiment.
